title: Утро после примирения  (The Morning After the Reconciliation)

segments.t: Waking up in Vika's bed the next morning, Max happily assumes that their night together means she has forgiven him and even suggests they fly away together as a couple. However, Vika quickly cools his enthusiasm, calling herself a fool for giving in to her emotions and reminding him that he cheated on her.
Это значит, что ты меня простила?
Я бы много могла простить, но не это.
Let's walk back through the scene line by line.
'I think so too.' Max stresses one familiar word in earnest: "dumayu" means "I think" (from "dumat"), giving the line its exact edge.

'Or maybe we really should?' Vika makes this point right away: Russian keeps the exact word order of a normal statement here, turning it into a question for Max purely through rising pitch at the end.
'Run away together as a couple.' Max fires back plainly across the room, letting the remark speak for itself.
Это значит, что ты меня простила?
'Does this mean that you have forgiven me?' Vika centers one classic word right here: "prostila" means "would forgive" (from "prostit"), giving the line its exact edge.
'It means that I am a fool.' Max makes this warning on cue: notice how Russian needs no word for "am", "is", or "are" in the present — placing the words side by side says it all.
'I gave in to my emotions.' Vika weighs in frankly with a nod, watching Max's face to see how the news lands.
'And what happens next?' Max stresses one vivid word right here: "dalshe" means "next, go on", and it carries the main weight of what Max is saying.
'Max, you cheated on me.' Vika puts the comeback frankly here: spoken Russian trims this down to just 4 words, dropping the extra helper words that English has to spell out.
Я бы много могла простить, но не это.
'I could have forgiven a lot, but not that.' Vika cuts in frankly with a sigh, leaving no doubt about where she stands.
'Well then...' Vika shares that line at once: spoken Russian trims this down to just 2 words, dropping the extra helper words that English has to spell out.
'The subject is closed.' Max aims this update frankly here: notice how Russian needs no word for "am", "is", or "are" in the present — placing the words side by side says it all.
'But we have not finished talking yet.' Vika steps in promptly as they talk, so Max knows she is not just making small talk.
'I will be back.' Max features this sharp term on cue: "yeshche" means "still" (from "yeshchyo"), giving the line its exact edge.
Это значит, что ты меня простила?
Я бы много могла простить, но не это.

That wraps up this scene as max wakes up with Vika hoping she has forgiven him and suggests flying away together, but Vika insists that giving in to emotion does not erase his infidelity. See you next time!
